title: This activist lives the real-world struggle of ‘Bloom Where You Are Planted’
summary: Acquitted after five years in prison, activist Amanda Echanis shows that the human rights message of the award-winning documentary ‘Bloom Where You Are Planted’ doesn't stop when the film ends

blocks.text: For 38-year-old peasant organizer Amanda Echanis, activism is both a personal calling and an inherited legacy. As a leader for the Cagayan provincial chapter of AMIHAN, she carries a deep history of resisting injustice — a fight woven into her family bloodline.

Echanis’ life and struggle are central to Noni Abao’s documentary Bloom Where You Are Planted, alongside fellow activists Agnes Mesina and the late Randy Malayao. The powerful film, which chronicles state repression and land rights in the Cagayan Valley, recently swept the 49th Gawad Urian Awards, taking home four major trophies: Best Film, Best Documentary, Best Direction, and Best Editing.

On December 2, 2020, state forces raided Echanis’ home in Baggao, Cagayan, arresting her on trumped-up charges of illegal possession of firearms and explosives. She was sent to prison alongside her then-one-month-old infant son, Randall Emmanuel.

Her quest for justice faced repeated pre-trial delays, extending her detention to over five years. Finally, on January 14, 2026, the Tuguegarao City Regional Trial Court Branch 10 acquitted Echanis after the prosecution failed to prove her guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

“Masaya na malaya na ako, kasama ang aking anak, matapos mapawalang-sala sa mga gawa-gawang paratang na ipinapataw sa mga katulad kong aktibista at artista ng bayan,” Echanis shared through PanitikanPH, a project of the UP Institute of Creative Writing.
(I’m happy that I’m free, with my son, after my acquittal from the fabricated charges imposed on activists and artists like me.)

“Narito sa aking patuloy na pagkilos, patuloy na paglikha, patuloy na paglilingkod sa kapwa lalo na sa mga batayang sektor sa lipunan at lalo na sa patuloy na pagsusulat — dito ko nahahanap ang aking paghinga, sa ideya na nagpapatuloy ako at hindi kailanman humupa sa pagkilos sa kabila ng pagkakapiit.”

(It’s through my continued action, my ongoing creation, my persistent service to others — especially to the marginalized sectors of society — and especially through my constant writing, that I find my breathing space. I will never back down despite the imprisonment.)

Echanis inherited her fierce commitment to social justice from her parents. Her father, prominent peasant leader and peace consultant Randall Echanis, was brutally murdered in his Manila home in August 2020.
Through the human rights organization Karapatan, Amanda continues to urge the public to hold the government accountable for her father’s unsolved killing.

Her mother, Linda Echanis, has long stood in solidarity with the movement. In a striking historical parallel, Amanda was first detained with her parents when she was just two years old following her father’s arrest on identical fabricated charges — making her the country’s youngest political prisoner at the time.
Additionally, her lineage extends to her uncle, Emmanuel Lacaba, a renowned activist-poet who joined the New People’s Army and was killed in South Cotabato in 1976.
An artist who uses literature as a weapon for advocacy, Echanis graduated from the Philippine High School for the Arts.

While in prison, she re-enrolled remotely at the University of the Philippines Diliman to finish her degree in Creative Writing. Making history in May 2025, she became the first political prisoner to run for and win a seat on the UP Diliman Student Council, topping the councilor race via remote video campaign calls.

As a writer, her published works focus heavily on land reform, human rights, and social justice. Her notable pieces include Nanay Mameng, a stage play depicting urban poverty through the eyes of an 86-year-old activist, Tatlong Paslit na Alaala, and her prison poetry collection, Binhi ng Paglaya.

In Bloom Where You Are Planted, the audience hears a moving recording of Echanis reading a poem about her parents’ activism, alongside a poignant clip of her assuring her son that “this, too, shall pass.”
Reflecting on the documentary’s success, Echanis stresses that its relevance is far from over.
“Ang pinaka-memorable na part ng pagpapalabas ng ‘Bloom Where You Are Planted’ ay hindi ito nagtatapos na kasaysayan,” she told Rappler.
“Ito ay nagpapatuloy pa rin hanggang sa kasalukuyan ang mga pagpapalabas ng pelikula sa iba’t ibang mga unibersidad, mga pagawaan, at mga sakahan, at kung nasaan ang mga simpleng mga mamamayan.”

(The most memorable part of Bloom Where You Are Planted is that it is not finished history. Film screenings continue to this day in various universities, workplaces, and farms — wherever the ordinary citizens are.)
With the youth making up a massive portion of today’s advocates, Echanis actively encourages them to use their creativity to amplify vulnerable sectors.
“‘Wag tayong matakot na alamin ang mga nangyayari sa lipunan, na paglingkuran ‘yung mga pinakamahihirap na sektor sa ating bansa — ang mga magsasaka,“ she said.
(Don’t be afraid to know what is happening in society. And don’t be afraid to serve the poorest sectors of our country — the farmers.) – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.
